solution:
Test the successive ratios: \(\frac{6}{2} = 3\), \(\frac{18}{6} = 3\), \(\frac{54}{18} = 3\).

The ratio is the same throughout, so the sequence is a G.P. with \(a = 2\), \(r = 3\).

\(t_n = ar^{n-1} = 2(3)^{n-1}\)

Yes, it is a G.P. and \(t_n = 2(3)^{n-1}\)

Test the successive ratios: \(\frac{-5}{1} = -5\), \(\frac{25}{-5} = -5\), \(\frac{-125}{25} = -5\).

The ratio is constant, so the sequence is a G.P. with \(a = 1\), \(r = -5\).

\(t_n = ar^{n-1} = 1 \cdot (-5)^{n-1}\)

Yes, it is a G.P. and \(t_n = (-5)^{n-1}\)

Test the successive ratios: \(\dfrac{1/\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{1}{5}\), \(\dfrac{1/(5\sqrt{5})}{1/\sqrt{5}} = \frac{1}{5}\), \(\dfrac{1/(25\sqrt{5})}{1/(5\sqrt{5})} = \frac{1}{5}\).

The ratio is constant, so the sequence is a G.P. with \(a = \sqrt{5}\), \(r = \frac{1}{5}\).

\(t_n = ar^{n-1} = \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}\)

Yes, it is a G.P. and \(t_n = \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}\)

Test the successive ratios: \(\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\frac{5}{4}\).

Since \(\frac{4}{3} \ne \frac{5}{4}\), the ratio is not constant.

The sequence is not a G.P. (its successive differences are all \(1\), so it is an A.P.)

Test the successive ratios: \(\frac{14}{7} = 2\) and \(\frac{21}{14} = \frac{3}{2}\).

Since \(2 \ne \frac{3}{2}\), the ratio is not constant.

The sequence is not a G.P. (its successive differences are all \(7\), so it is an A.P.)

If three numbers are in G.P., the middle one is their geometric mean, so its square equals the product of the other two.

\(x^{2} = \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{4}{27} = \frac{16}{81}\)

\(x = \pm\sqrt{\frac{16}{81}} = \pm\frac{4}{9}\)

Both values work: \(x = \frac{4}{9}\) gives \(r = \frac{1}{3}\) and \(x = -\frac{4}{9}\) gives \(r = -\frac{1}{3}\).

\(x = \pm\frac{4}{9}\)

\(t_n = \frac{5^{n-3}}{2^{n-3}} = \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{n-3}\)

Then \(\dfrac{t_n}{t_{n-1}} = \dfrac{(5/2)^{n-3}}{(5/2)^{n-4}} = \frac{5}{2}\), which is the same for every \(n\).

Since the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, the sequence is a G.P.

First term: \(t_1 = \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{-2} = \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{2} = \frac{4}{25}\).

\(t_1 = \frac{4}{25}\), \(r = \frac{5}{2}\)

Let the three numbers be \(\frac{a}{r},\ a,\ ar\).

Sum: \(a\left(\frac{1}{r} + 1 + r\right) = 21\), i.e. \(\frac{a(1+r+r^{2})}{r} = 21\).

Sum of squares: \(\frac{a^{2}(1+r^{2}+r^{4})}{r^{2}} = 189\).

Using \(1+r^{2}+r^{4} = (1+r+r^{2})(1-r+r^{2})\) and dividing the second equation by the square of the first:

\(\frac{1-r+r^{2}}{1+r+r^{2}} = \frac{189}{441} = \frac{3}{7}\)

\(7 - 7r + 7r^{2} = 3 + 3r + 3r^{2}\)

\(4r^{2} - 10r + 4 = 0\), i.e. \(2r^{2} - 5r + 2 = 0\), so \(r = 2\) or \(r = \frac{1}{2}\).

For \(r = 2\): \(a\left(\frac{1}{2}+1+2\right) = 21 \Rightarrow \frac{7a}{2} = 21 \Rightarrow a = 6\), giving \(3,\ 6,\ 12\).

For \(r = \frac{1}{2}\) the same numbers appear in reverse order.

The numbers are \(3,\ 6,\ 12\) or \(12,\ 6,\ 3\)

Let the four numbers be \(\frac{a}{r^{3}},\ \frac{a}{r},\ ar,\ ar^{3}\) (common ratio \(r^{2}\)).

Product: \(\frac{a}{r^{3}} \cdot \frac{a}{r} \cdot ar \cdot ar^{3} = a^{4} = 1\), so \(a = 1\) (taking the real positive value).

Sum of the middle two: \(\frac{1}{r} + r = \frac{10}{3}\)

\(3r^{2} - 10r + 3 = 0\), so \(r = 3\) or \(r = \frac{1}{3}\).

For \(r = 3\): \(\frac{1}{27},\ \frac{1}{3},\ 3,\ 27\); for \(r = \frac{1}{3}\) the same numbers in reverse order.

The numbers are \(\frac{1}{27},\ \frac{1}{3},\ 3,\ 27\) or \(27,\ 3,\ \frac{1}{3},\ \frac{1}{27}\)

Let the G.P. have first term \(a\) and common ratio \(R\). Then

\(x = t_5 = aR^{4}\), \(y = t_8 = aR^{7}\), \(z = t_{11} = aR^{10}\).

\(y^{2} = \left(aR^{7}\right)^{2} = a^{2}R^{14}\)

\(xz = aR^{4} \cdot aR^{10} = a^{2}R^{14}\)

Both sides are equal, so \(y^{2} = xz\) is verified.

Since \(p, q, r, s\) are in G.P., let the common ratio be \(k\). Then \(q = pk\), \(r = pk^{2}\), \(s = pk^{3}\).

\(p + q = p(1+k)\)

\(q + r = pk + pk^{2} = pk(1+k)\)

\(r + s = pk^{2} + pk^{3} = pk^{2}(1+k)\)

Ratios of consecutive terms: \(\dfrac{q+r}{p+q} = \dfrac{pk(1+k)}{p(1+k)} = k\) and \(\dfrac{r+s}{q+r} = \dfrac{pk^{2}(1+k)}{pk(1+k)} = k\).

Both ratios equal \(k\), so \(p+q,\ q+r,\ r+s\) are in G.P. with common ratio \(k\).

The count doubles each hour, so it forms a G.P. with common ratio \(2\), starting from \(50\) bacteria at the start (after \(0\) hours).

Number after \(n\) hours \(= 50(2)^{n}\).

At the end of the \(5^{\text{th}}\) hour, \(n = 5\):

\(50 \times 2^{5} = 50 \times 32 = 1600\)

There will be \(1600\) bacteria at the end of the \(5^{\text{th}}\) hour
_note: DISAGREES WITH THE PRINTED KEY, which gives 800. 800 is \(50 \times 2^{4}\), obtained by taking the original 50 as the FIRST TERM \(t_1\) and then quoting \(t_5 = ar^4 = 800\), i.e. conflating 'the 5th term' with 'the end of the 5th hour'. But 50 is the count at the START (0 hours elapsed), so the end of the 5th hour is 5 doublings later: 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. The book's OWN convention elsewhere in this same exercise confirms the exponent equals the number of periods elapsed: Q12 gives the nth bounce as \(80(3/4)^n\) (80 ft is the drop, not a bounce) and Q14 gives the population after n years as \(200(1.1)^n\) (200 is the initial count). Applying that same rule here gives \(50 \times 2^5 = 1600\). Book key appears to be an off-by-one; flagged for maintainer adjudication.

solution:
The ball falls \(80\) ft and each rebound is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the height it has just fallen, so the rebound heights form a G.P.

First rebound \(= 80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\), second rebound \(= 80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}\), and so on.

Height on the \(n^{\text{th}}\) bounce \(= 80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{n}\) ft.

On the \(6^{\text{th}}\) bounce: \(80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{6} = 80 \times \frac{729}{4096} = \frac{3645}{256} \approx 14.24\) ft.

The ball rebounds \(80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{6}\) ft on the \(6^{\text{th}}\) bounce and \(80\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{n}\) ft on the \(n^{\text{th}}\) bounce

For three numbers in G.P., the square of the middle term equals the product of the other two.

\(x^{2} = 3(x+6)\)

\(x^{2} - 3x - 18 = 0\)

\((x-6)(x+3) = 0\)

\(x = 6\) or \(x = -3\)

A growth of \(10\%\) a year multiplies the population by \(1 + \frac{10}{100} = 1.1\) each year, so the yearly counts form a G.P. with \(r = 1.1\) starting from \(200\).

Number after \(3\) years \(= 200(1.1)^{3} = 200 \times 1.331 = 266.2\).

Number of mosquitoes after \(3\) years \(= 200(1.1)^{3} \approx 266\)

Each year the population is multiplied by \(1.1\), so after \(10\) years it is \(200(1.1)^{10}\).

\((1.1)^{10} \approx 2.5937\), so \(200(1.1)^{10} \approx 518.7\).

Number of mosquitoes after \(10\) years \(= 200(1.1)^{10} \approx 519\)

Each year multiplies the population by \(1.1\), so after \(n\) years the initial \(200\) has been multiplied by \(1.1\) exactly \(n\) times.

Number of mosquitoes after \(n\) years \(= 200(1.1)^{n}\)

For three numbers in G.P., the square of the middle term equals the product of the other two.

\((2x)^{2} = (x-6)x^{2}\)

\(4x^{2} = x^{3} - 6x^{2}\)

\(x^{3} - 10x^{2} = 0\), i.e. \(x^{2}(x-10) = 0\), so \(x = 0\) or \(x = 10\).

\(x = 0\) is rejected because it makes the second and third terms \(0\), and no term of a G.P. can be zero.

\(x = 10\)

With \(x = 10\), the first term is \(x - 6\).

\(x - 6 = 10 - 6 = 4\)

First term \(= 4\)

Here \(a = 3\) and \(r = \frac{6}{3} = 2 > 1\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{a\left(r^{n}-1\right)}{r-1} = \dfrac{3\left(2^{n}-1\right)}{2-1}\)

\(S_n = 3\left(2^{n}-1\right)\)

Here \(a = p\) and \(r = \frac{q}{p}\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{a\left(1-r^{n}\right)}{1-r} = \dfrac{p\left[1-\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}\right]}{1-\frac{q}{p}} = \dfrac{p\left[1-\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}\right]}{\frac{p-q}{p}}\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{p^{2}}{p-q}\left[1-\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}\right]\) when \(q < p\).

If \(q > p\) then \(r > 1\) and the same working with \(\dfrac{a\left(r^{n}-1\right)}{r-1}\) gives \(\dfrac{p^{2}}{q-p}\left[\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}-1\right]\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{p^{2}}{p-q}\left[1-\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}\right]\) if \(q < p\), and \(S_n = \dfrac{p^{2}}{q-p}\left[\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{n}-1\right]\) if \(q > p\)

Here \(a = \sqrt{5}\) and \(r = \dfrac{-5}{\sqrt{5}} = -\sqrt{5}\) (check: \(-5 \times -\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{5}\)).

\(S_n = \dfrac{a\left(r^{n}-1\right)}{r-1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}\left[\left(-\sqrt{5}\right)^{n}-1\right]}{-\sqrt{5}-1}\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{-\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}+1}\left[\left(-\sqrt{5}\right)^{n}-1\right]\)

Let the G.P. be \(a, ar, ar^{2}, \ldots\)

Sum of the first three terms: \(a + ar + ar^{2} = a\left(1+r+r^{2}\right) = 125\).

Sum of the next three terms: \(ar^{3} + ar^{4} + ar^{5} = ar^{3}\left(1+r+r^{2}\right) = 27\).

Dividing the second by the first: \(r^{3} = \dfrac{27}{125}\)

\(r = \frac{3}{5}\)

The terms are not in G.P., so first write each term using \(9, 99, 999, \ldots\)

\(S_n = 3 + 33 + 333 + \cdots = \frac{3}{9}\left(9 + 99 + 999 + \cdots \text{ to } n \text{ terms}\right)\)

\(= \frac{3}{9}\left[\left(10-1\right) + \left(10^{2}-1\right) + \cdots + \left(10^{n}-1\right)\right]\)

\(= \frac{3}{9}\left[\left(10 + 10^{2} + \cdots + 10^{n}\right) - n\right]\)

The bracketed sum is a G.P. with \(a = 10\), \(r = 10\): it equals \(\dfrac{10\left(10^{n}-1\right)}{9}\).

\(S_n = \frac{3}{9}\left[\dfrac{10\left(10^{n}-1\right)}{9} - n\right]\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{3}{81}\left[10\left(10^{n}-1\right) - 9n\right]\)

Write each term using \(9, 99, 999, \ldots\)

\(S_n = 8 + 88 + 888 + \cdots = \frac{8}{9}\left(9 + 99 + 999 + \cdots \text{ to } n \text{ terms}\right)\)

\(= \frac{8}{9}\left[\left(10 + 10^{2} + \cdots + 10^{n}\right) - n\right]\)

The G.P. inside gives \(\dfrac{10\left(10^{n}-1\right)}{9}\), so

\(S_n = \frac{8}{9}\left[\dfrac{10\left(10^{n}-1\right)}{9} - n\right]\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{8}{81}\left[10\left(10^{n}-1\right) - 9n\right]\)

\(S_n = 0.4 + 0.44 + 0.444 + \cdots = \frac{4}{9}\left(0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + \cdots \text{ to } n \text{ terms}\right)\)

\(= \frac{4}{9}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right) + \left(1-\frac{1}{10^{2}}\right) + \cdots + \left(1-\frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

\(= \frac{4}{9}\left[n - \left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

The G.P. inside has \(a = \frac{1}{10}\), \(r = \frac{1}{10}\), so it equals \(\dfrac{1}{9}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\).

\(S_n = \frac{4}{9}\left[n - \frac{1}{9}\left(1-\frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{4}{81}\left[9n - \left(1-\dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

\(S_n = 0.7 + 0.77 + 0.777 + \cdots = \frac{7}{9}\left(0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + \cdots \text{ to } n \text{ terms}\right)\)

\(= \frac{7}{9}\left[n - \left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

The G.P. inside sums to \(\dfrac{1}{9}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\), so

\(S_n = \frac{7}{9}\left[n - \frac{1}{9}\left(1-\frac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{7}{81}\left[9n - \left(1-\dfrac{1}{10^{n}}\right)\right]\)

This is a G.P. with \(a = 0.5 = \frac{5}{10}\) and \(r = \frac{0.05}{0.5} = \frac{1}{10} < 1\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{a\left(1-r^{n}\right)}{1-r} = \dfrac{\frac{5}{10}\left[1-\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{n}\right]}{\frac{9}{10}}\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{5}{9}\left[1-\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^{n}\right]\)

This is a G.P. with \(a = 0.2 = \frac{2}{10}\) and \(r = \frac{0.02}{0.2} = \frac{1}{10} < 1\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{a\left(1-r^{n}\right)}{1-r} = \dfrac{\frac{2}{10}\left[1-\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{n}\right]}{\frac{9}{10}}\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{2}{9}\left[1-\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^{n}\right]\)

For \(n \ge 2\), \(t_n = S_n - S_{n-1}\).

\(t_n = 2\left(3^{n}-1\right) - 2\left(3^{n-1}-1\right) = 2 \cdot 3^{n} - 2 \cdot 3^{n-1} = 2 \cdot 3^{n-1}(3-1) = 4(3)^{n-1}\)

For \(n = 1\): \(t_1 = S_1 = 2(3-1) = 4\), which also equals \(4(3)^{0}\), so the formula holds for all \(n\).

Now \(\dfrac{t_n}{t_{n-1}} = \dfrac{4(3)^{n-1}}{4(3)^{n-2}} = 3\), a constant, so the sequence is a G.P. with \(a = 4\), \(r = 3\).

\(t_n = 4(3)^{n-1}\)

Let the G.P. be \(a, ar, ar^{2}, \ldots, ar^{n-1}\).

Sum: \(S = \dfrac{a\left(r^{n}-1\right)}{r-1}\).

Product: \(P = a^{n} \cdot r^{1+2+\cdots+(n-1)} = a^{n}r^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\).

Sum of reciprocals: \(R = \dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{ar} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{ar^{n-1}}\), a G.P. with first term \(\frac{1}{a}\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{r}\), so

\(R = \dfrac{\frac{1}{a}\left(1-\frac{1}{r^{n}}\right)}{1-\frac{1}{r}} = \dfrac{r^{n}-1}{a\,r^{n-1}(r-1)}\).

Hence \(\dfrac{S}{R} = \dfrac{a\left(r^{n}-1\right)}{r-1} \times \dfrac{a\,r^{n-1}(r-1)}{r^{n}-1} = a^{2}r^{n-1}\).

\(\left[\dfrac{S}{R}\right]^{n} = a^{2n}r^{n(n-1)}\) and \(P^{2} = \left(a^{n}r^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\right)^{2} = a^{2n}r^{n(n-1)}\).

Both sides are equal, so \(\left[\dfrac{S}{R}\right]^{n} = P^{2}\) is verified.

Let the G.P. have first term \(a\) and ratio \(r\), and write \(A = \dfrac{a}{r-1}\), so that \(S_m = A\left(r^{m}-1\right)\).

\(S_n = A\left(r^{n}-1\right)\)

\(S_{2n} - S_n = A\left(r^{2n}-r^{n}\right) = A\,r^{n}\left(r^{n}-1\right)\)

\(S_{3n} - S_{2n} = A\left(r^{3n}-r^{2n}\right) = A\,r^{2n}\left(r^{n}-1\right)\)

LHS \(= S_n\left(S_{3n}-S_{2n}\right) = A\left(r^{n}-1\right) \times A\,r^{2n}\left(r^{n}-1\right) = A^{2}r^{2n}\left(r^{n}-1\right)^{2}\)

RHS \(= \left(S_{2n}-S_n\right)^{2} = \left[A\,r^{n}\left(r^{n}-1\right)\right]^{2} = A^{2}r^{2n}\left(r^{n}-1\right)^{2}\)

LHS \(=\) RHS, so \(S_n\left(S_{3n}-S_{2n}\right) = \left(S_{2n}-S_n\right)^{2}\) is verified.

\(\sum_{r=1}^{10}\left(3 \times 2^{r}\right) = 3\left(2 + 2^{2} + \cdots + 2^{10}\right)\)

The bracket is a G.P. with first term \(2\), ratio \(2\) and \(10\) terms:

\(2 + 2^{2} + \cdots + 2^{10} = \dfrac{2\left(2^{10}-1\right)}{2-1} = 2(1024-1) = 2046\)

\(\therefore\) the sum \(= 3 \times 2046 = 6138\)

\(6138\)

\(\sum_{r=1}^{10}\left(5 \times 3^{r}\right) = 5\left(3 + 3^{2} + \cdots + 3^{10}\right)\)

The bracket is a G.P. with first term \(3\), ratio \(3\) and \(10\) terms:

\(3 + 3^{2} + \cdots + 3^{10} = \dfrac{3\left(3^{10}-1\right)}{3-1} = \dfrac{3}{2}\left(3^{10}-1\right)\)

\(\therefore\) the sum \(= 5 \times \dfrac{3}{2}\left(3^{10}-1\right) = \dfrac{15}{2}\left(3^{10}-1\right) = 442860\)

\(\dfrac{15}{2}\left[3^{10}-1\right]\)

An appreciation of \(5\%\) a year multiplies the value by \(1.05\) each year, so the yearly values form a G.P. with \(r = 1.05\).

Value after \(6\) years \(= 15\left(1.05\right)^{6}\) Lac.

Using the given \((1.05)^{6} = 1.34\):

\(15 \times 1.34 = 20.1\)

The house is worth Rs. \(20.1\) Lac after \(6\) years

At \(8\%\) compound interest the amount is multiplied by \(1.08\) each year, so after \(n\) years the amount is \(10000(1.08)^{n}\).

To double the money: \(10000(1.08)^{n} = 20000\), i.e. \((1.08)^{n} = 2\).

Using the given \((1.08)^{5} = 1.47\):

\((1.08)^{10} = \left[(1.08)^{5}\right]^{2} = (1.47)^{2} = 2.1609 \approx 2\)

\(\therefore\) \(n = 10\).

It takes about \(10\) years to double the money
